title: Most multiway systems grow exponentially or not at all

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Most multiway systems grow exponentially or not at all

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Most multiway systems (which keep all sequences produced by all possible replacements at each step) either grow exponentially fast or do not grow at all; slow growth is rare.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: most either grow exponentially quickly, or not at all; slow growth of the kind seen on the facing page is rather rare.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 5, “Two Dimensions and Beyond”; section “Multiway Systems” (from p. 204), p. 207. Scope: multiway (non-deterministic string rewriting) systems with simple rules

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch05-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.71

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The growth statistic is measurable, but the population and rarity threshold require choices not fixed by the claim. Exhaustive computation is feasible only for bounded rule spaces, so the unrestricted generalization is only partially resolved.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate a prespecified finite grammar of simple string-replacement systems, measure distinct-state growth, and classify growth as zero, subexponential, or exponential. The observed proportions and their stability as rule size increases test whether slow growth is rare.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Finite runs can misclassify long transients.

“Most” depends on a sampling measure over rules.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.55
data existence: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.72
discriminating power: 0.72
operationalizability: 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: State counts are a direct observable, and small rules can be simulated with public software, so a finite census is a real test. The claim quantifies over multiway systems in general, while only very small rules stay computable, and the fast-growing majority is exactly what the state explosion hides. Ensemble choice and the cutoff for slow growth keep a sample from settling the full quantifiers.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate a declared family of short string-rewriting rules, plot the number of distinct strings against step, and classify each run as bounded, slowly growing, or exponential. A large intermediate class would challenge the claim; a strong two-way split would support it inside that family.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The fraction called rare moves when the distribution over rule size and alphabet changes.

A short run can make polynomial growth look exponential.

Fast growth exhausts memory, so the systems that are easiest to classify are the slow ones.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.58
analysis feasibility: 0.48
operationalizability: 0.62
data adequacy: 0.45
data existence: 0.7
